body.objective: Students will be able to feel compound metre.
successCriteria: I can tell simple metre from compound metre
I can count and perform rhythms in 6/8
I can recognize compound metre in music
body.hook: Clap along to a jig, a lullaby or many Celtic and folk tunes, and you'll notice the beat seems to bounce in threes: ONE-two-three, FOUR-five-six. That bouncing feel comes from compound metre, and it's a different way of organizing time from most pop songs.

vocabulary.definition: The way beats are grouped in music.
A metre where each beat divides into two, such as 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4.
A metre where each beat divides into three, such as 6/8.
A compound metre with six eighth notes per bar, felt as two main beats.
In 6/8, the note that lasts one main beat (three eighth notes).

study.title: Twos and Threes
study.question: How is compound metre different from simple metre?
study.passage:
Simple vs compound:
• Simple metre (2/4, 3/4, 4/4): each beat splits into two eighth notes: "1-and 2-and."
• Compound metre (6/8): each beat splits into three eighth notes: "1-la-li 2-la-li."
In 6/8 there are six eighth notes per bar, but you feel two main beats, on eighth notes 1 and 4. A dotted quarter note lasts one main beat.
Part 1, Feel it (5 minutes): Count "1-2-3-4-5-6" with accents on 1 and 4 while stepping on the accents.
Part 2, Compare (10 minutes): The teacher plays two short clips: one in 4/4 (a march or pop song) and one in 6/8 (a jig or a lullaby). Students step to each and describe the difference. Public-domain examples in 6/8 include "Pop Goes the Weasel" and "Row, Row, Row Your Boat."
Part 3, Read (10 minutes), in 6/8:
Line 1: dotted quarter, dotted quarter
Line 2: three eighth notes, dotted quarter
Line 3: quarter, eighth, quarter, eighth
Line 4: six eighth notes
Part 4, Create (10 minutes): In pairs, write a two-bar rhythm in 6/8 and perform it over a classmate playing dotted quarter notes on a drum.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; "Pop Goes the Weasel" and "Row, Row, Row Your Boat" are traditional songs in the public domain.

body.objective: Students will be able to perform rhythms from world traditions.
body.iCan: I can perform rhythms from world traditions.
successCriteria: I can perform a rhythm pattern from a world music tradition
I can keep my part steady while others play different patterns
I can describe where a rhythm comes from and how it is used
body.hook: In Havana, Accra and Rio, music is built on interlocking rhythm patterns that everyone in the group knows by heart. Learn one pattern and you can join in; learn three and you can feel how a whole drum circle fits together.

vocabulary.definition: A key rhythm pattern in Cuban music, also the name of the two sticks that play it.
A repeating timeline played on a bell that guides West African drumming.
A repeating pattern the whole group follows.
A short pattern repeated over and over.
A leader plays or sings a phrase and the group answers.
A repeating rhythmic cycle in Indian classical music.

study.title: Rhythms of the World
study.question: How do different traditions organize rhythm?
study.passage:
Rhythm stations (written for this lesson; patterns shown on a counting grid, x = play, . = rest):
1. Cuba, son clave 3-2 (two bars of 4/4 in eighths): bar 1: x . . x . . x . (1, the "and" of 2, 4); bar 2: . . x . x . . . (2, 3). Play on claves or clap while the group steps the beat. Clave is the guide pattern in son and salsa.
2. West Africa, the 12/8 bell pattern (Ewe tradition, Ghana and Togo): x . x . x x . x . x . x over 12 pulses. Play on a cowbell or agogo while others play a low drum on pulses 1, 4, 7 and 10.
3. Brazil, samba: the low surdo drum accents beat 2 of each 2/4 bar; shakers play steady sixteenths.
4. India, Teentaal: a 16-beat cycle grouped 4+4+4+4. Clap on beats 1, 5 and 13, and wave the hand (khali, the "empty" section) on beat 9.
Rotate through stations, then perform two patterns layered together. Respect tip: these rhythms belong to living traditions; name the culture and the instrument each time you perform.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; patterns are widely taught in music education.

discussion: Which pattern was hardest to keep steady, and why?

body.objective: Students will be able to create a polyrhythm.
successCriteria: I can explain what a polyrhythm is
I can create a short polyrhythmic piece in a group
body.hook: Tap your left hand twice while your right hand taps three times in the same space. That tug between two patterns is a polyrhythm, and it powers music from West African drumming to modern jazz and electronic music.

vocabulary.definition: Two or more different rhythms played at the same time, each dividing the same span differently.
Three even notes in one part against two even notes in another, over the same time span.
A shift between groupings of 2 and 3 within a metre.
A rhythm that cuts across the main beat.
One part in a stack of rhythms.
A row of equal pulses used to line up rhythms.

study.title: Two Rhythms at Once
study.question: How do polyrhythms work, and how can I create one?
study.passage:
Building 3 against 2 (written for this lesson):
1. Make a grid of 6 equal pulses: 1 2 3 4 5 6.
2. Part A (the "3"): play on 1, 3 and 5.
3. Part B (the "2"): play on 1 and 4.
4. Together: both hands on 1, right on 3, left on 4, right on 5. A popular memory phrase is "hot cup of tea": "hot" (both), "cup" (right), "of" (left), "tea" (right).
5. Practise slowly: one hand at a time, then together on a desk, then on drums or body percussion.
6. Hear it: 3 against 2 is common in West African and Afro-Cuban music; 6/8 bars that switch to feel like 3/4 create hemiola.
7. Create (20 minutes): In groups of four, build a 12-pulse grid. Layer a 2-part, 3-part, 4-part and 6-part pattern (12 ÷ 2, 3, 4, 6). Add one accent pattern of your own. Perform for 8 cycles with a clear start and ending.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
